title: Coins and dice: why many tosses are easier to guess than one

summary.text: Nobody can say whether the next coin toss will land heads or tails. But toss a coin 20 times, and heads comes up close to 10 times. Do it again, and again it is close to 10. Roll a die 30 times, and a six comes up only about 5 times, because a die has six faces and the six is only one of them. Each single toss or roll is a surprise. Many of them together follow a pattern we can count on. Chance is how likely something is when we cannot know for sure.
summary.art: A child sitting on a bed with a steel tumbler and a coin, and a tally sheet beside her with two rows of marks, one for heads and one for tails, almost the same length.

intro.hook: Hold a coin. Before you drop it on the bed, say 'heads' or 'tails'. Were you right? Try again. Can you get it right every time?
intro.text: Some things we can say for sure. The Sun will rise tomorrow. A dropped spoon will fall down. Other things we cannot know, like how the next coin toss will land. In this unit you toss coins and roll a die many times, and keep count. You find out that one toss is a surprise, but many tosses are not. You also learn the words likely, unlikely, certain and impossible, and play games that are fair and games that are not.
intro.art: A girl's hand opening over a bed, with a coin just landed, and a thought bubble with 'heads?' and 'tails?' in it.

outcomes: By the end I can say that nobody can know how one coin toss will land, but that many tosses give close to half heads.
By the end I can toss a coin many times, keep a tally and count heads and tails.
By the end I can show that a six is unlikely on one roll of a die, and say why.
By the end I can sort things into certain, likely, unlikely and impossible.
By the end I can say whether a game is fair, and change an unfair game to make it fair.
By the end I can say why, after many heads in a row, the next toss is still just as likely to be heads or tails.

terms.meaning: Chance is how likely something is to happen, when we cannot know for sure.
terms.example: There is a good chance of rain in Kochi in July, because that is the monsoon. There is very little chance of snow in Chennai.
terms.art: A window with monsoon rain falling outside, and a child holding an umbrella by the door.

terms.meaning: To toss a coin is to throw it, flip it or shake it, so that it lands without anyone choosing how.
terms.example: Shake a coin in a covered steel tumbler and tip it onto the bed. That is a toss.
terms.art: A hand covering the top of a steel tumbler, shaking it, with a coin inside.

terms.meaning: Heads and tails are the names of the two sides of a coin. On an Indian coin, we call the side with the lions heads and the side with the number tails.
terms.example: If the lions are on top after the toss, it is heads.
terms.art: Two Indian coins side by side, one showing the four-lion emblem and one showing the number side.

terms.meaning: A die is a small cube with a different number of dots on each of its six faces, from 1 to 6. Two or more are called dice.
terms.example: In Ludo you roll one die to see how many squares to move.
terms.art: A white die on a Ludo board, with the five face on top.

terms.meaning: Likely means it will happen more often than not. Unlikely means it will happen less often than not.
terms.example: When you roll a die, getting a number that is not six is likely. Getting a six is unlikely.
terms.art: A die showing a six, next to five dice showing 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.

terms.meaning: Certain means it will happen for sure. Impossible means it can never happen.
terms.example: Rolling a number from 1 to 6 on a die is certain. Rolling a 7 on one die is impossible.
terms.art: A die with a big green tick next to it, and beside it the number 7 crossed out in red.

terms.meaning: A game or a choice is fair when everyone has the same chance.
terms.example: Tossing a coin to choose who goes first is fair. Each person has the same chance.
terms.art: Two children standing on either side of a coin in the air, one calling heads and one calling tails.

terms.meaning: A tally is a quick way to count with lines. You draw one line for each thing, and every fifth line goes across the four before it.
terms.example: Five heads in a tally look like four standing lines with one line across them.
terms.art: A tally of 12 on paper: two bundles of five with a line across each, and two single lines.

terms.meaning: To predict is to say what will happen before it happens.
terms.example: You can predict that in 20 tosses, heads will come up about 10 times.
terms.art: A girl pointing at a blank tally sheet, with a thought bubble that says 'about 10 heads'.

explanations.concept: Why nobody can know how one toss will land
explanations.context: This card explains what you found when you tried to guess single coin tosses.
explanations.definition: How a coin lands depends on its spin, its height and how it hits the bed. These change a tiny bit with every toss, too little to see or control. So nobody can know how one toss will land.
explanations.description: When you guessed ten tosses, you were right about half the time. Most people are, however hard they try. The shake, the spin and the bounce are a little different each time, and nobody can see or control that. So for one toss, heads and tails each have the same chance.
examples: Guessing heads or tails before each toss in the coin test
Calling heads or tails before a cricket match
Rolling a die in Ludo and hoping for a six
explanations.art: A coin tumbling through the air above a bed, with tiny curved arrows showing it spinning, and a question mark above it.

explanations.concept: Why many tosses give close to half heads
explanations.context: This card explains why everyone's 20 tosses gave close to 10 heads.
explanations.definition: Each toss has the same chance of heads as of tails. So when you toss many times, about half the tosses come up heads. The more tosses you make, the closer to half it usually gets.
explanations.description: Nobody could say how any one toss would land. Yet your 20 tosses gave close to 10 heads, and so did your grown-up's. Some tosses gave heads and some gave tails, and they balanced out. Scientists call this the law of large numbers. The more tosses we count, the closer heads gets to half of all the tosses.
examples: Adding the family's tosses together and getting close to half heads
John Kerrich, a mathematician, tossed a coin 10,000 times and got 5,067 heads
explanations.art: Two tally sheets side by side, each with a heads row and a tails row of almost the same length, labelled 'Amma' and 'me'.

explanations.context: This card explains the four words we use to say how likely something is.
explanations.definition: Certain means it will happen for sure. Likely means it will happen more often than not. Unlikely means it will happen less often than not. Impossible means it can never happen.
explanations.description: A die has six faces, and only one face has six dots. In the six test, a six came up only about once in every six rolls, so a six is unlikely. The other five faces together came up about five times in every six rolls, so 'not a six' is likely. Some things are certain, like getting a number from 1 to 6. Some are impossible, like a 7 on one die.
examples: Certain: the Sun rises tomorrow morning
Likely: rain on a July day in Kochi, during the monsoon
Unlikely: a six on one roll of a die
explanations.art: A line drawn across the page from 'impossible' on the left to 'certain' on the right, with a die showing 7 crossed out at the left end, a die showing six near the left, a pile of not-six dice near the right, and a sunrise at the right end.

explanations.context: This card explains what fair means in a game of chance.
explanations.definition: A game of chance is fair when every player has the same chance of winning. It is unfair when one player's chance is bigger.
explanations.description: In the slips game, 8 slips had a star and only 2 were blank, so a star came out most times. If you win on a star and your friend wins on a blank, the game is unfair. To make it fair, use the same number of star slips and blank slips. A coin is fair because both sides have the same chance. A die is fair because all six faces have the same chance.
examples: Tossing a coin to choose who bats first
5 star slips and 5 blank slips in a tumbler
A race where one player moves on a six and the other moves on any other number, which is unfair
explanations.art: Two steel tumblers of folded slips: one with eight star slips and two blank ones, labelled 'unfair', and one with five of each, labelled 'fair'.

explanations.context: This card explains a mistake that many grown-ups make too.
explanations.definition: The chance of heads is the same on every toss, whatever came before. After many heads in a row, tails is not any more likely than before.
explanations.description: Suppose you toss four heads in a row. Many people then feel sure the next toss must be tails. But nothing about the last four tosses changes how the next one spins and lands. Heads and tails still have the same chance. Over many tosses they even out because new tosses keep coming, not because tails catches up. In the same way, after five rolls with no six, a six is not 'due'. It is still about one chance in six.
examples: Four heads in a row, and the next toss is still half and half
Waiting for a six in Ludo: it does not come sooner because you have waited
A long run of tails in the coin test
explanations.art: A row of four coins all showing heads, then a fifth coin in the air with a question mark, and a sign under it saying 'still half and half'.

explanations.concept: Is there such a thing as luck?
explanations.context: This card is about a question people have argued about for a very long time.
explanations.description: Many people say some days, numbers or hands are lucky. When scientists test coins and dice, a 'lucky' hand gets the same counts as any other hand over many tosses. But people do differ in other ways, and scientists are still studying what people mean by luck.
examples: A cricket captain who says she is lucky at the toss
A 'lucky number' for a Ludo roll
Blowing on the dice before rolling

perspectives.explanation: Some people, days or numbers are lucky. A lucky person wins the toss more often.

perspectives.who: Scientists who test coins and dice
perspectives.explanation: When anyone tosses many times, heads comes up close to half. No hand, number or wish has been shown to change that.
He studied people who call themselves lucky. He found they often notice chances that others miss, and try more new things. So 'luck' may partly be how a person meets the world.

explanations.art: A boy blowing on a die in his hand before a Ludo roll, while his sister holds a tally sheet.

agreed.text: Nobody can know how one toss of a coin will land.
agreed.evidence: In the coin test, guesses were right only about half the time, however hard people tried.

agreed.text: When a coin is tossed many times, heads comes up close to half the time.
agreed.evidence: In the coin test, each person's 20 tosses gave close to 10 heads. John Kerrich tossed a coin 10,000 times and got 5,067 heads.

agreed.text: On a fair die, each face comes up about once in every six rolls, so a six is unlikely on one roll.
agreed.evidence: In the six test, 30 rolls gave only a few sixes and many more not-sixes.

agreed.text: Past tosses do not change the chance of the next toss.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have tested this with very many tosses. After a run of heads, the next toss is still heads about half the time.

challenging.claim: After many heads in a row, tails is due, so the next toss will probably be tails.
challenging.who: Many people think this, including many grown-ups.
challenging.for: Over many tosses, heads and tails come out close to half each. So it feels as if tails must catch up.
challenging.against: Each toss starts fresh. After a run of heads, the next toss is still heads about half the time. The counts even out because of the many new tosses, not because tails catches up.
challenging.context: This card is about a mistake so common that it has a name: the gambler's mistake.

challenging.claim: A six is half and half, because it either comes or it does not.
challenging.who: Many children, and some grown-ups, think this.
challenging.for: There are two things that can happen: a six, or not a six.
challenging.against: 'Not a six' is five faces, and 'a six' is only one face. In the six test, not-sixes came up many more times than sixes.
challenging.context: This card is about a common way of counting chances that goes wrong.

challenging.claim: A coin tossed by hand lands heads exactly half the time and tails exactly half the time.
challenging.for: A coin has two sides that are almost the same weight, and heads and tails come up close to half each.
challenging.against: Persi Diaconis, Susan Holmes and Richard Montgomery studied coin tosses and said a coin tossed by hand should land on the side it started on a little more often. In 2023, a team tossed coins over 350,000 times and found this: about 51 times in 100. The difference is tiny, too small to see in 20 tosses.
challenging.context: This card is about a surprise found by tossing coins a very large number of times.

big_questions.q: You could not guess one toss, but you could guess 20 tosses well. How can we know more about many tosses than about one?
big_questions.hint: Think of what happened to the tally rows as they grew longer.

big_questions.q: If someone could see exactly how fast your coin was spinning, could they say how it would land?
big_questions.hint: What decides how a coin lands? Is it chance, or the spin, the height and the bounce?

big_questions.q: Is luck real, or is it only chance that we cannot follow?
big_questions.hint: Think about the 'lucky' hand in the coin test. Did its counts look different?

big_questions.q: Would life be better if we could know everything that will happen tomorrow?
big_questions.hint: Think of a game where you always know who will win. Would anyone play it?

big_questions.q: Is the weather forecast 'likely rain' a good guess, even on a day it does not rain?
big_questions.hint: Likely does not mean certain. What would make the forecast a good one over many days?

how_we_found_out.story: For hundreds of years, people said a coin lands heads half the time. A few people tested it by tossing a coin a very large number of times. John Kerrich was a mathematician from South Africa. During the Second World War, he was held in a prison camp in Denmark. With a lot of time in the camp, he tossed a coin 10,000 times, and his friend Eric Christensen helped him keep count. He got 5,067 heads, very close to half. But most people also thought a coin tossed by hand is perfectly half and half. In 2007, Persi Diaconis, Susan Holmes and Richard Montgomery, scientists in the United States, studied coin tosses with fast cameras. They said a coin tossed by hand should land on the side that started on top a little more often. In 2023, a team of 48 people led by František Bartoš tossed coins over 350,000 times. They found it: the starting side came up about 51 times in every 100. The coin is very close to fair, but not exactly.
how_we_found_out.who: John Kerrich, a South African mathematician. Persi Diaconis, Susan Holmes and Richard Montgomery, who study mathematics and statistics in the United States. A team led by František Bartoš.
how_we_found_out.when: Kerrich's 10,000 tosses during the Second World War, published in 1946. Diaconis, Holmes and Montgomery in 2007. The 350,000 tosses in 2023.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a coin tossed by hand is exactly half and half. Very many tosses showed it lands on its starting side a tiny bit more often, about 51 times in 100.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in a prison camp hut tossing a coin onto a table, while his friend writes long rows of tally marks in a notebook.

story.title: Meera, Kiran and the Six That Would Not Come
story.note: Meera, Kiran and their Amma are made up. Amma means mother in Malayalam and many other Indian languages.
text: Meera was nine, and she lived in Kochi with her Amma and her little brother Kiran. Kiran was six.
It was July, and the monsoon rain had been falling for three days. Nobody could go out to play. So Amma took the Ludo board down from the top of the cupboard.
Kiran picked the green counters. Meera picked the red. In their house, a counter could leave home only when you rolled a six.
Meera rolled first. Three. Kiran rolled. Two. Meera rolled a six on her third turn, and her first red counter stepped out onto the board.
Kiran rolled again. Four. Then one. Then five. His green counters sat at home, waiting.
"This die doesn't like me," said Kiran. He blew on the die. He shook it for a long time. He whispered, "Six, six, six," and rolled. It was a two.
"Blowing on it does not change anything," said Meera. "I'll show you."
She tore a page out of her notebook. She drew two rows. One row said 'six'. The other row said 'not six'.
"We will roll thirty times," she said. "Each time, I make a line in the right row. You roll."
Kiran rolled. Three. Meera drew a line in the 'not six' row. Five. Another line. One. Another line. Then a six. Kiran cheered, and Meera drew a line in the 'six' row.
They rolled and rolled. The rain drummed on the window. Amma brought them banana chips in a steel bowl.
After thirty rolls, they counted. The 'six' row had five lines. The 'not six' row had twenty-five.
"See?" said Meera. "A six came about once in every six rolls. The die has six faces, and only one of them is a six. The other five faces are all 'not six'."
Kiran looked at the die. He turned it in his fingers. One, two, three, four, five, and six. "So a six is hard to get," he said.
"It is unlikely," said Meera. "But it does come. If you roll many times, it comes about once in six."
They went back to the game. Kiran rolled. Four. Two. One. Three. Five.
"Five rolls and no six!" said Kiran. "So the next one must be a six. It has to come now."
Meera thought about it. It did feel like the six was coming. Then she remembered something Amma had told her.
"The die starts fresh every time," she said. "Each roll has the same chance as every other roll. Waiting does not make a six come sooner."
Kiran rolled. Two.
"You see?" said Meera, and they both laughed.
Kiran rolled again, and this time it was a six. His first green counter stepped out of home at last.
"I knew it!" said Kiran.
"You did not know it," said Meera, smiling. "Nobody knows the next roll. But I knew that, if you kept rolling, a six would come about once in six."
That evening, Amma asked them who had won. "Meera won," said Kiran. "But I found out a secret. You can't know one roll. You can know lots of rolls."
Amma smiled. "That is the secret people who study chance found too," she said. "Weather people use it. When they say rain is likely tomorrow, they cannot be sure. But they know what usually happens."
Outside, the rain went on falling. Nobody knew when it would stop. But everyone in Kochi knew it was likely to rain again tomorrow.
story.epiphany: Nobody can know the next roll of a die. But over many rolls, a six comes up about once in every six, because only one of the six faces is a six. And waiting does not make a six come sooner: each roll starts fresh.
ask: Why did Kiran's blowing on the die not help him get a six?
Meera's tally had 5 sixes and 25 not-sixes. Why were there so many more not-sixes?
After five rolls with no six, Kiran said a six must come next. Was he right? Why?
Kiran said, 'You can't know one roll. You can know lots of rolls.' What did he mean?
When the weather forecast says rain is likely, and it does not rain, was the forecast wrong?

experiments.title: The Coin Test: can you guess the toss?
experiments.context: In this experiment you try to guess ten coin tosses, one at a time. Then you and a grown-up each toss a coin 20 times and count the heads. You find out what you can and cannot guess.
experiments.question: Can we guess how one coin toss will land? Can we guess how many heads will come in 20 tosses?
experiments.predict: Before you start: how many of your ten guesses will be right? And in 20 tosses, how many heads will come? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Everyone uses the same kind of coin and tosses it the same way: shake it in a covered tumbler and tip it onto the bed. Nobody looks inside or chooses how it lands. We toss 20 times each, because a few tosses can be a fluke. Two people toss, so we can see if the counts come out close.

materials.item: a steel tumbler or a cup
a bed, a mattress or a folded towel to tip onto
paper and a pencil for the tally

schedule.what: Guess ten tosses. Then toss 20 times each and tally heads and tails.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Keep the tally sheets. Circle the person whose heads count was closest to 10.

setup.caption: 2. Shake it and tip it onto the bed.

flow.do: 1. Show your child a coin. 2. Agree that the side with the lions is heads and the number side is tails. 3. Show how to toss. Drop the coin in the tumbler and cover it with a hand. Shake three times and tip it onto the bed.
flow.say: This side, with the lions, is heads. This side, with the number, is tails. Watch how we toss. Shake, shake, shake, and tip.
flow.kid: The lions side is heads. The number side is tails. Shake the tumbler three times. Tip it onto the bed.
flow.parent: Tipping onto a bed or towel stops the coin rolling away under the furniture. A shaken coin cannot be steered, so the toss is fair.
flow.context: This is the first step of the coin test. You learn how to toss fairly.

flow.do: 1. Ask the two questions below. 2. Write down your child's guesses and reasons at the top of the paper.
flow.say: Before each toss, you will say heads or tails. Out of ten guesses, how many will you get right? And if we toss 20 times, how many heads will come? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How many of ten guesses will you get right? In 20 tosses, how many heads? Why?

ask.q: How many of your ten guesses will be right? Why?
good: All ten, because I will think hard.
About five, because it could be either.
I don't know, because nobody can see inside the tumbler.

flow.parent: Write the guesses down and do not say who is right. Many children expect to get most guesses right, or expect 20 heads if they 'want' heads.
flow.context: In this step of the coin test, you make your predictions.

flow.do: 1. Before each toss, your child says heads or tails out loud. 2. Your child tosses. 3. Mark a tick if the guess was right and a cross if it was wrong. 4. Do this ten times. 5. Count the ticks.
flow.say: Say your guess first. Now toss. Were you right? Make a tick or a cross. Let's do ten.
flow.kid: Say heads or tails. Toss. Right or wrong? Make a mark.

ask.q: How many did you get right? Could you get better by trying harder?
good: About half. Trying harder did not help.
Sometimes right, sometimes wrong. I could not tell.

flow.parent: Most children get between 3 and 7 right. That is what guessing gives. If your child gets 8 or more, do ten more guesses. The count usually comes back towards 5.
flow.context: In this step of the coin test, you try to guess ten tosses.

flow.do: 1. Draw two rows on a new paper: heads and tails. 2. Your child tosses 20 times and makes a tally line in the right row each time. 3. You toss 20 times on a second paper. 4. Use tally bundles of five.
flow.say: Now we stop guessing and just count. Toss 20 times. Each time, make a line in the heads row or the tails row. Then it is my turn.
flow.kid: Toss 20 times. Each time, make a line in the right row.
flow.parent: Count the tosses as you go so you stop at 20. Bundles of five make counting easy at the end.
flow.context: In this step of the coin test, each person tosses 20 times and keeps a tally.

flow.do: 1. Count the heads and tails on each sheet. 2. Fill in the results table. 3. Ask the questions below. 4. Then read the cards on why nobody can know one toss, and why many tosses give close to half.
flow.say: How many heads did you get? How many did I get? Were they close to 10? Could you guess each toss? Why was the total easier to guess than one toss?
flow.kid: Count your heads. Count mine. Are they close to 10? Why?

ask.q: Why could we guess the total better than one toss?
good: Heads and tails each came about the same number of times.
Each toss was a surprise, but they evened out.
Half of 20 is 10, and we got close to 10.

check.q: In the coin test, you tossed 20 times. What did the heads count come out close to?
check.why: Heads and tails each have the same chance, so about half the tosses are heads. Half of 20 is 10. A count near 20 would mean the coin always lands heads, and it does not.

flow.parent: Counts between 7 and 13 are normal for 20 tosses. If one count is far from 10, such as 5 or 15, toss 20 more and add them in. A strong answer uses both sheets as evidence: neither total was far from 10, but nobody could guess each toss.
flow.context: This is the last step of the coin test. You count and say what you found.

experiments.title: The Six Test: is a six half and half?
experiments.context: In this experiment you roll a die 30 times. You keep a tally of how many times you roll a six, and how many times you roll something else.
experiments.question: When we roll a die, does a six come up as often as all the other numbers together?
experiments.predict: In 30 rolls, which will come up more: a six, or not a six? Or will they be the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use one die and roll it the same way each time, onto the same bed or tray. We roll 30 times, because a few rolls can be a fluke. Nobody blows on the die or chooses how it lands.

materials.item: one die, for example from a Ludo or snakes and ladders set. If you have none, use a six-sided pencil with the numbers 1 to 6 written near one end, one on each side.
a tray, a bed or a folded towel to roll onto

schedule.what: Roll a die 30 times and tally sixes and not-sixes.

experiments.record: Draw two rows, 'six' and 'not six'. Make a tally line for every roll. Write the two totals. Draw a bar for each total.

flow.do: 1. Give your child the die. 2. Ask them to count the faces and the numbers on them. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: How many faces does this die have? How many of them show a six? If we roll 30 times, will we get more sixes, or more not-sixes, or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count the faces. How many show six? Will six or not six come more? Why?

ask.q: Which will come up more in 30 rolls: six, or not six? Why?
good: Not six, because five faces are not six.
The same, because it is either six or not six.
Six, because I want a six.

flow.parent: Write the guess and the reason down. 'The same, because it either comes or it doesn't' is a very common idea. The test will answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the six test. You look at the die and guess.

flow.do: 1. Draw two rows on the paper: 'six' and 'not six'. 2. Your child rolls the die onto the tray. 3. Your child makes a tally line in the right row. 4. Roll 30 times in all. Count the rolls as you go.
flow.say: Roll the die. Is it a six? Make a line in the six row. Is it any other number? Make a line in the not-six row. Let's do 30 rolls.
flow.kid: Roll. Six or not six? Make a line in the right row. Do 30.

ask.q: After ten rolls, which row is longer?
good: The not-six row.
The not-six row, by a lot.

flow.parent: A die that falls on the floor can be rolled again. If you use a six-sided pencil, roll it gently across the table and read the side facing up.
flow.context: In this step of the six test, you roll the die 30 times.

flow.do: 1. Count each row. 2. Draw a bar for each total. 3. Ask the questions below. 4. Then read the card on likely, unlikely, certain and impossible.
flow.say: How many sixes did you get? How many not-sixes? Which is likely, and which is unlikely? Why do you think there were so many more not-sixes?
flow.kid: Count each row. Which is likely? Which is unlikely? Why?

ask.q: Why were there so many more not-sixes?
good: Five faces are not six, and only one is six.
A six is only one face out of six.

check.q: In the six test, why did not-six come up many more times than six?
options: The die does not like sixes
Five of the six faces are not six
check.why: The die has six faces and each has the same chance. Five faces are 'not six' and one face is 'six'. So in 30 rolls, about 5 are sixes and about 25 are not.

flow.parent: Usually 2 to 8 sixes come up in 30 rolls, and many more not-sixes. A strong answer counts the faces: one six against five other faces.
flow.context: This is the last step of the six test. You count and explain.

activities.title: Sure or Not Sure? A spoon and a coin
activities.context: In this activity you drop a spoon and toss a coin. You say what you are sure will happen and what you are not sure about. It is a way in before the coin test.

schedule.what: Drop a spoon and toss a coin. Say what you were sure of and what you were not.

activities.record: Say out loud one thing you are sure of and one thing you are not sure of. A grown-up writes them down.

setup.art: A child letting go of a steel spoon above a bed, with an arrow pointing down.
setup.caption: 1. Drop a spoon. Were you sure it would fall?

setup.art: A coin landing on a bed, and the child looking at it with a puzzled face.
setup.caption: 2. Toss a coin. Were you sure how it would land?

flow.do: 1. Hold a spoon above the bed. 2. Ask your child where it will go when you let go. 3. Let go.
flow.say: If I let go of this spoon, what will happen? Are you sure? Let's see.
flow.kid: Will the spoon fall if I let go? Are you sure?
flow.parent: Your child is sure the spoon will fall, and is right. Do not explain anything yet.

flow.do: 1. Show your child a coin. 2. Ask whether it will land lions up. 3. Toss it onto the bed.
flow.say: Now this coin. Will it land with the lions up? Are you sure, like with the spoon?
flow.kid: Will the coin land lions up? Are you sure?

ask.q: Why were you sure about the spoon, but not the coin?
good: The spoon always falls down.
The coin can land either way.
I can't see how the coin will land.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to name one more thing at home they are sure about. 2. Then one thing they are not sure about.
flow.say: Tell me one thing in our home that you are sure will happen today. Now tell me one thing you are not sure about.
flow.kid: Say one thing you are sure of. Say one thing you are not sure of.

ask.q: What are you not sure about today?
good: Whether it will rain.
Which crow will come to the window.
What is for dinner.

flow.parent: Good answers for 'sure': the fan turns when switched on, water runs from the tap. For 'not sure': rain, how many crows come to the window, a game's winner.

activities.title: The Slips Game: what is likely to come out?
activities.context: In this activity you fold ten paper slips. Eight have a star and two are blank. You pick one without looking, ten times, and see which kind comes out more.

materials.item: a sheet of paper cut into ten slips the same size
a steel tumbler or a small bowl

schedule.what: Make 8 star slips and 2 blank slips. Pick one ten times. Then make a fair set.

activities.record: Tally stars and blanks for ten picks. Then tally again with 5 of each.

setup.art: Ten small paper slips on a table, eight with a star drawn on them and two blank.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a star on 8 slips. Leave 2 blank.

setup.art: Folded slips in a steel tumbler and a child's hand reaching in, eyes looking away.
setup.caption: 2. Fold them. Mix them. Pick one without looking.

setup.art: A tally sheet with a long row for stars and a short row for blanks.
setup.caption: 3. Make a tally line. Put the slip back. Pick ten times.

flow.do: 1. Cut ten slips the same size. 2. Your child draws a star on eight of them. 3. Leave two blank. 4. Fold them all the same way and put them in the tumbler.
flow.say: Draw a star on eight slips. Leave two blank. Fold them all the same, so you cannot tell them apart.
flow.kid: Draw stars on eight slips. Leave two blank. Fold them all.
flow.parent: Folding them the same way stops anyone from feeling which is which.

flow.do: 1. Ask the question below.
flow.say: If you pick one slip without looking, will it more likely be a star or a blank? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Will you pick a star or a blank? Why?

ask.q: Which is more likely: a star or a blank? Why?
good: A star, because there are more stars.
A blank, because I want a blank.

flow.do: 1. Shake the tumbler. 2. Your child picks one slip without looking and opens it. 3. Make a tally line. 4. Put the slip back, folded. 5. Do this ten times.
flow.say: Shake, pick and open. Star or blank? Put it back and shake again. Let's do ten.
flow.kid: Shake. Pick one without looking. Star or blank? Put it back.
flow.parent: Putting the slip back each time keeps the chances the same for every pick. Expect about 8 stars, often between 6 and 10.

flow.do: 1. Count the tally. 2. Ask the question below. 3. Take out three star slips and add three blank slips. 4. Pick ten more times.
flow.say: You win on a star. I win on a blank. Is that fair? How can we make it fair? Let's try with five of each.
flow.kid: Is this game fair? How could we make it fair?

ask.q: How can we make the game fair?
good: Put in the same number of stars and blanks.
Five stars and five blanks.

check.q: A tumbler has 8 star slips and 2 blank slips. You pick one without looking. What is most likely?
check.why: There are four times as many star slips as blank ones, so a star comes out much more often. 'Both just as likely' would be true only with the same number of each.

flow.parent: With five of each, stars and blanks come out about the same number of times. That is a fair game.

activities.title: Toss Ten Coins at Once
activities.context: In this activity you shake ten coins together and tip them out. You count the heads. You do it five times and see what number comes up most.

materials.item: a steel tumbler or a dabba with a lid
a bed or a folded towel

schedule.what: Shake ten coins together five times. Count the heads each time.

activities.record: Write the number of heads after each shake. Circle the number that came most.

setup.art: Ten coins in a steel dabba with the lid on, held in two small hands.
setup.caption: 1. Put ten coins in a dabba. Close the lid and shake.

setup.art: Ten coins spread out on a bedsheet, some lions up and some number up, with the lions-up coins pushed into a small group.
setup.caption: 2. Tip them out. Push the heads to one side and count them.

flow.do: 1. Put ten coins in the dabba. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: When we tip out ten coins, how many will land heads? Will it be the same every time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How many of ten coins will land heads? Why?

good: About five, half of ten.
I can't know for sure.

flow.do: 1. Your child shakes and tips out the coins. 2. Counts the heads. 3. You write the number. 4. Do it five times.
flow.say: Shake and tip. Push the heads to one side. How many? Let's do it five times.
flow.kid: Shake and tip. Count the heads. Do it five times.
flow.parent: Expect numbers like 4, 5 and 6 most often, and sometimes 3 or 7. Ten heads at once is very rare.

flow.do: 1. Look at the five numbers. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at our numbers. Were they all the same? Which numbers were they close to?
flow.kid: Were the numbers the same each time? What were they close to?

ask.q: What were the numbers close to?
good: Close to five.
Half of ten.

games.title: Certain, Likely, Unlikely, Impossible: a card game
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or 1 player sorting alone
games.context: This is a card game about chance. Each card says something that might happen. You decide whether it is certain, likely, unlikely or impossible.

items.f: You roll one die and get a number from 1 to 6.
items.b: Certain. Every face has a number from 1 to 6.

items.f: You roll one die and get a 7.
You roll one die and get a six.
items.b: Unlikely. Only one face of six is a six.

items.f: You roll one die and do not get a six.
items.b: Likely. Five faces of six are not six.

items.f: You toss ten coins and all ten land heads.
A dropped spoon falls up to the ceiling.
It rains on a July day in Kochi.
items.b: Likely. July is in the monsoon in Kerala.

items.f: It snows on Marina Beach in Chennai.
items.b: Impossible, as far as anyone knows. Chennai is far too warm for snow.

items.f: You pick a star from a tumbler with 8 star slips and 2 blank ones.
items.b: Likely. Most slips have a star.

items.f: You pick a blank from a tumbler with 8 star slips and 2 blank ones.
A crow comes to a window in a city flat some time this week.
items.b: Likely. Crows live in almost every Indian city.

items.f: Your fan turns when you switch it on, and the power is on.
items.b: Likely, almost certain. It turns unless it is broken.

items.f: Water put in the freezer turns to ice by tomorrow.
items.b: Certain, if the freezer is working.

items.f: A coin lands on its edge and stays standing.
items.b: Unlikely. It can happen, but very, very rarely.

items.f: You toss a coin 20 times and get heads 18 times or more.
items.b: Unlikely. In 20 tosses, heads usually comes close to 10.

rules: Cut out the 16 happening cards. Shuffle them and put them face down in a pile.
Each player gets four sign cards: Certain, Likely, Unlikely and Impossible.
One player turns over the top card and reads it out.
Everyone puts down one sign card, face down. Then everyone turns their sign over at the same time.
Read the back of the happening card. Everyone who matched it gets a point. Anyone who disagrees can give a reason, and the others decide if it is a good one.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most points wins. Playing alone, sort the cards into four piles and then check the backs.

setup.art: A pile of small cards face down, and three children each holding four sign cards: Certain, Likely, Unlikely, Impossible.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the cards. Each player takes four signs.

setup.art: A girl reading a card that says 'You roll one die and get a six', while two children put down 'Unlikely'.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Put down a sign. Turn the signs over together.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards together. 2. Read the rules out loud. 3. Put the four sign cards in a row, from impossible to certain.
flow.say: Each card is something that might happen. Is it certain, likely, unlikely or impossible? Put down your sign, and we turn them over together.
flow.kid: Read the card. Is it certain, likely, unlikely or impossible? Put down a sign.

flow.do: 1. Take turns reading a card. 2. Everyone puts down a sign. 3. Turn the signs over and read the back. 4. Give points.
flow.say: You roll one die and get a six. Which sign? Why did you choose that?
flow.kid: Read a card. Put down a sign. Check the back.

ask.q: Why is a six on one roll unlikely, and not impossible?
good: It can happen, but only one face is a six.
It came up a few times in the six test.

options: Rolling a six on one die
check.why: A six and heads can both happen, so they are not impossible. No face of a die has 7 dots, so a 7 can never come.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Which card was the hardest to decide? Why?
flow.kid: Which card was the hardest? Why?

ask.q: Why is a coin standing on its edge unlikely, and not impossible?
good: It can happen, but it almost never does.
A coin has a thin edge, so it could stay standing.

games.title: The Six Race: is this game fair?
games.context: This is a race game with one die. At first, one player moves only on a six, and the other moves on any other number. You find out whether that is fair, and then change the rules to make it fair.

printables.title: A race track of 10 squares for each player, from Start to Finish

rules: Take turns to roll one die. Whoever rolls, the counters move by these rules.
First rules: if the die shows a six, Player A moves one square. If it shows any other number, Player B moves one square.
The first counter to reach Finish wins.
Play once with the first rules. Then talk about whether it was fair.
New rules: Player A moves on 1, 2 or 3. Player B moves on 4, 5 or 6. Play again.

setup.art: Two race tracks of ten squares side by side on paper, with a button on each Start square and a die beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Draw two tracks of ten squares. Put a counter on each Start.

setup.art: A die showing four dots, and a hand moving Player B's counter one square forward.
setup.caption: 2. Roll. Move the counter the rules say.

flow.do: 1. Draw the two tracks, or use the printed board. 2. Use buttons or coins as counters. 3. Let your child choose to be Player A or Player B.
flow.say: Player A moves on a six. Player B moves on any other number. Which player do you want to be? Why?
flow.kid: Pick Player A or Player B. Why that one?

ask.q: Which player do you think will win? Why?
good: B, because B moves on five numbers.
A, because six is the best number.

flow.parent: If your child picks A because 'six is the best', let them. The game will show what happens.

flow.do: 1. Take turns rolling. 2. Move the right counter after each roll. 3. Play until one counter reaches Finish.
flow.say: Roll. Is it a six? Then A moves. Any other number? Then B moves.
flow.kid: Roll. Six moves A. Any other number moves B.
flow.parent: B almost always wins, often by a long way. A six comes only about once in six rolls.

flow.do: 1. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Who won? Was the game fair? Why not? How could we change the rules so each player has the same chance?
flow.kid: Was it fair? How could we make it fair?

ask.q: How could we make the game fair?
good: Give each player three numbers.
A moves on 1, 2, 3 and B on 4, 5, 6.
A moves on odd numbers, B on even numbers.

flow.do: 1. Play again with the new rules: A moves on 1, 2 or 3, and B moves on 4, 5 or 6.
flow.say: Now each player has three numbers. Who will win this time? Can you tell before we start?
flow.kid: Play again. Each player has three numbers now. Who will win?

check.q: Player A moves on 1, 2 or 3. Player B moves on 4, 5 or 6. Is the game fair?
options: Yes, each player has three faces of the die
No, B always wins because B has bigger numbers
No, A always wins because A has smaller numbers
check.why: Each face has the same chance. Three faces each means the same chance each. Bigger numbers do not come up more often than smaller ones.

flow.parent: Now either player can win. Nobody can say who will win before the game starts. That is what a fair game of chance is like.

projects.title: One Hundred Tosses: a three-day count
projects.context: In this project you toss a coin 100 times in all, over three days. Each day you add your tosses to the total. You watch how close the heads count gets to half.

materials.item: a coin and a steel tumbler
a notebook page for the tally

schedule.what: Toss 30 times. Tally heads and tails. Write the totals.
Toss 30 more times. Add them to day 1.
Toss 40 more times to reach 100. Add up all the heads and tails.

projects.record: A tally page with heads and tails rows for each day, and a box at the bottom for the totals out of 100.

setup.art: A notebook page with three sections labelled Day 1, Day 2 and Day 3, each with a heads row and a tails row of tally marks.
setup.caption: 1. Make a tally page with a part for each day.

setup.art: A box at the bottom of the page reading 'Heads out of 100' and 'Tails out of 100', with numbers close to 50 written in.
setup.caption: 2. On day 3, add up all 100 tosses.

flow.do: 1. Your child tosses 30 times and keeps a tally. 2. Write the heads and tails totals for day 1.
flow.say: Today we toss 30 times. Tomorrow 30 more, then 40 more. How many heads will we have out of 100? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Toss 30 times. Tally heads and tails. How many heads out of 100 will you get? Why?

ask.q: How many heads will come out of 100? Why?
good: About 50, half of 100.
Close to 50, but not exactly.

flow.do: 1. Your child tosses 30 more times. 2. Add the new heads to day 1's heads, and the new tails to day 1's tails.
flow.say: Thirty more tosses today. Now add them to yesterday. How many heads have we got out of 60?
flow.kid: Toss 30 more. Add them to yesterday.

flow.do: 1. Your child tosses 40 more times. 2. Add up all the heads and all the tails. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Forty more, and we reach 100. How many heads out of 100? Was it close to 50? Was any single day exactly half?
flow.kid: Toss 40 more. Add up all the heads. Is it close to 50?

ask.q: Was the total closer to half than one day's count?
good: Yes, the days went up and down, but the total was near 50.
One day had more heads, another had more tails, and they evened out.

flow.parent: Totals between 40 and 60 heads are normal for 100 tosses. The point to notice is that each day's count wobbles, but the total out of 100 is close to half.

challenges.title: The Fair Chooser Challenge: choose fairly among three
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A coin is a fair way to choose between two people. But what if three children all want to go first?
challenges.problem: Make a fair way to choose one of three children, so each has the same chance, using things at home.
constraints: Each of the three children must have the same chance.
Nobody may choose or steer the result.
Use only things you find at home.
Test it at least 12 times and tally who gets chosen.
materials: a die or a six-sided pencil
three paper strips, one cut shorter
a pencil and paper for the tally
general: Three folded slips, one with each name, in a tumbler. Pick one without looking.
Roll a die. 1 or 2 chooses the first child, 3 or 4 the second, 5 or 6 the third.
creative: Draw straws. Hold three paper strips with the ends hidden, one cut shorter. Each child picks one. The child with the short strip is chosen.
Two coin tosses: heads-heads chooses one child, heads-tails another, tails-heads the third, and tails-tails means toss again.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own fair chooser. Use it 12 times and tally who is chosen. If one child is chosen far more often, change your design and test again.

setup.art: Three folded slips with names in a steel tumbler, and a die beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Find a way to give three children the same chance.

setup.art: A tally sheet with three rows labelled with three names, each with about four lines.
setup.caption: 2. Test it 12 times. Tally who is chosen.

flow.do: 1. Explain the problem. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: A coin has two sides, so it can choose between two people. How could we choose fairly among three?
flow.kid: A coin has two sides. How can you choose fairly among three children?

ask.q: How could you give three children the same chance?
good: Three slips with names in a tumbler.
Give each child two numbers on a die.

flow.do: 1. Your child makes a chooser. 2. Tests it 12 times. 3. Tallies who is chosen.
flow.say: Make your chooser. Use it 12 times. Make a tally line for whoever is chosen.
flow.kid: Make your chooser. Test it 12 times. Tally who is chosen.
flow.parent: With 12 tries, each child should be chosen about 4 times, often between 2 and 6. A chooser that picks one child 9 or more times is probably not fair.

flow.do: 1. Look at the tally. 2. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Was each child chosen about the same number of times? If not, why? How could you make it fairer?
flow.kid: Was each child chosen about the same? How could it be fairer?

check.q: You roll a die to choose among three children. Which rule is fair?
options: 1 chooses Asha, 2 chooses Bindu, 3 to 6 choose Chitra
1 or 2 chooses Asha, 3 or 4 chooses Bindu, 5 or 6 chooses Chitra
6 chooses Asha, any other number chooses Bindu
check.why: Each face has the same chance. Two faces each gives each child the same chance. In the other rules, one child gets more faces than the others.

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it means.
pairs: will happen more often than not
items.why: These are the four words the child needs to talk about chance. Certain and impossible are the two ends. Likely sits in between. Fair is about everyone having the same chance.

items.p: In the coin test, you guessed ten tosses. About how many guesses do most people get right?
items.why: Heads and tails each have the same chance, so a guess is right about half the time. Choosing 'all ten' means thinking that trying hard can tell you how the coin will land. The test shows it cannot.
items.context: This question is about the coin test. You guessed ten tosses of a coin, then each person tossed a coin 20 times and counted the heads.

items.p: Draw your tally from the coin test. Show the heads row and the tails row.
items.a: Two rows of tally lines, in bundles of five, of nearly the same length.
items.why: A strong drawing shows both rows close in length. That is the evidence that heads and tails came up about the same number of times.
items.context: This question is about the coin test. You guessed ten tosses of a coin, then each person tossed a coin 20 times and counted the heads.
items.art: An empty box with two lines, labelled 'heads' and 'tails'.

items.p: Sort these into 'likely' and 'unlikely'.
items: rolling a number that is not six
picking a star from 8 stars and 2 blanks
picking a blank from 8 stars and 2 blanks
rain on a July day in Kochi
ten heads when you toss ten coins
items.why: Likely things happen more often than not: five faces of a die are not six, most slips have stars, and July is monsoon time in Kerala. Unlikely things happen less often than not.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why could nobody guess how one coin toss would land?
items.a: Tiny differences in the shake, the spin and the bounce decide how it lands, and nobody can see or control them.
items.why: A strong answer names something about the toss that is too small or fast to see. Saying 'because it is luck' does not say what decides how the coin lands.
items.context: This question is about the coin test. You guessed ten tosses of a coin, then each person tossed a coin 20 times and counted the heads.

items.p: Ananya tossed a coin 20 times. 11 were heads. How many were tails?
items.why: 20 take away 11 is 9. So she got 11 heads and 9 tails, close to half each.
items.context: This question is about the coin test. You guessed ten tosses of a coin, then each person tossed a coin 20 times and counted the heads.

items.p: A die has six faces, and only one of them shows a six.
items.why: True. That is why a six comes up only about once in every six rolls.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 2, and her brother Arjun have tossed a coin four times. It landed heads all four times.

views.says: The next toss is still half and half. The coin starts fresh every time.
Tails has to come now. Heads and tails always even out.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Kavya, because each toss has the same chance whatever came before. It also says Arjun is right that over many tosses heads and tails come out close to half.
items.why: Arjun has part of it right: many tosses do even out. But they even out because of the many new tosses, not because tails must come next. A strong answer uses the coin test, where runs of heads or tails happened and then the next toss could go either way.

items.p: Look at the line from impossible to certain. Write each one where it belongs: 'roll a 7', 'roll a six', 'roll not a six', 'roll a number from 1 to 6'.
a: near the left: roll a six
near the right: roll not a six
right end: roll a number from 1 to 6
items.why: A 7 can never come, so it is impossible. A six is one face out of six, so it is unlikely. Not a six is five faces out of six, so it is likely. Some number from 1 to 6 always comes, so it is certain.
items.art: A long line with 'impossible' at the left end and 'certain' at the right end, and four empty label boxes along it.

items.p: Three of these are fair ways to choose who goes first. Which one is not fair?
opts: Pick one of two folded name slips
Roll a die: six means Meena goes first, any other number means Ravi goes first
Roll a die: odd means Meena, even means Ravi
items.why: In that rule, Ravi has five faces and Meena has only one, so Ravi almost always goes first. The others give each person the same chance.

items.p: Put the coin test in order.
items: Guess heads or tails before each toss
Toss 20 times and keep a tally
Count the heads and compare with 10
items.why: First you test whether you can guess single tosses. Then you count many tosses to see what the total is close to.
items.context: This question is about the coin test. You guessed ten tosses of a coin, then each person tossed a coin 20 times and counted the heads.

items.p: In the six test, you rolled a die 30 times. About how many sixes would you expect?
items.why: A six is one face out of six. One sixth of 30 is 5. Choosing 15 means thinking a six is half and half. The six test shows it is not.
items.context: This question is about the six test. You rolled a die 30 times and made a tally of sixes and not-sixes.

items.p: Many people think a six is half and half, because it either comes or it does not. What would you tell them? Use the six test.
items.a: I would tell them that 'not six' is five faces and 'six' is only one face. In the six test, we got only a few sixes and many more not-sixes.
items.why: A strong answer counts faces and uses the tally as evidence. Two things that can happen do not always have the same chance.
items.context: This question is about the six test. You rolled a die 30 times and made a tally of sixes and not-sixes.

items.p: Draw two tumblers of slips: one where a star is likely, and one where a star and a blank are just as likely.
items.a: One tumbler with many star slips and few blank ones. One tumbler with the same number of each.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that what is in the tumbler decides the chance. More star slips make a star more likely.
items.context: This question is about the slips game. You put 8 slips with a star and 2 blank slips in a tumbler, and picked one without looking, ten times.
items.art: Two empty tumbler outlines side by side.

items.p: Before a cricket match, the two captains toss a coin to choose who bats first. Shalini says the toss is fair. Her friend Farhan says the toss is not fair, because his team lost it three times this month.

views.says: The toss is fair. Each captain has the same chance every time.
It can't be fair if we keep losing it.

views.who: Scientists who toss coins many times
views.says: A tossed coin is very close to fair, but lands on the side that started on top a tiny bit more often, about 51 times in 100.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Shalini, because losing three tosses in a row can happen with a fair coin. It may say the scientists found a tiny lean, too small to matter in a few tosses. It says Farhan is right that it is worth checking a game is fair.
items.why: Runs of losses happen by chance, so three losses do not show the toss is unfair. The scientists' lean is real but tiny, about 1 toss in 100. A strong answer weighs what each view gets right.

items.p: If you toss a coin 20 times, you always get exactly 10 heads.
items.why: False. You get close to 10, such as 8, 9, 11 or 12, but not always exactly 10. Each toss is a surprise, so the total wobbles a little.

items.p: Sort these into 'fair' and 'unfair'.
items: A moves on 1, 2, 3 and B on 4, 5, 6
A moves on a six and B on any other number
calling heads or tails on a coin
items.why: A game is fair when each player has the same chance. Equal numbers of slips, or equal numbers of die faces, give the same chance. Unequal numbers make one side more likely to win.

items.p: In the Six Race with the first rules, Player A moves on a six and Player B moves on the other numbers. How many faces of the die help Player B?
items.why: The die has six faces. One is six, so the other five help Player B. That is why B nearly always wins.
items.context: This question is about the Six Race game, where a die decides which counter moves.

items.p: Kiran rolled five times with no six. He says a six must come next. Is he right? Why?
items.a: No. Each roll starts fresh, so a six is still about one chance in six. Waiting does not make it come sooner.
items.why: A strong answer says the chance is the same on every roll. It may add that over many rolls a six comes about once in six, but no single roll is 'due'.

items.p: Look at Revathi's bar chart from the six test. Label the bar that is 'likely' and the bar that is 'unlikely'.
labels: the tall bar for not six
a: tall bar for not six: likely
items.why: The six bar is short because a six is one face out of six. The not-six bar is tall because five faces are not six. A taller bar means it happened more often.
items.context: This question is about the six test. You rolled a die 30 times and made a tally of sixes and not-sixes.

items.p: The weather forecast for Mumbai says rain is likely tomorrow. Tomorrow it does not rain. What does this mean?
opts: The forecast must have been wrong
Likely is not certain, so a dry day can still happen
items.why: Likely means more often than not, not every time. A good forecast of 'likely rain' is right on most such days, not on all of them. Choosing 'wrong' mixes up likely and certain.

quiz.p: Can anyone know for sure how one coin toss will land?
opts: Yes, if they blow on it
quiz.why: Tiny differences in the shake, spin and bounce decide it, and nobody can see or control them. Thinking hard or blowing on the coin does not change this.

quiz.p: Revathi tosses a coin 20 times. About how many heads will she get?
quiz.why: Heads and tails have the same chance, so about half of 20 tosses are heads. Half of 20 is 10.

quiz.p: What is a quick way to count with lines, in bundles of five?
quiz.why: A tally is a line for each thing, with every fifth line across the four before it. It helps you count tosses without losing track.

quiz.p: You roll one die. Which is most likely?
quiz.why: Five of the six faces are not six, so 'not a six' comes most often. A seven is impossible on one die.

quiz.p: Why is a six unlikely on one roll of a die?
opts: Only one of the six faces is a six
The die is scared of sixes
quiz.why: Each face has the same chance, and only one face is a six. So a six comes about once in every six rolls.

opts: Rolling a number from 1 to 6 on one die
quiz.why: Every face of a die has a number from 1 to 6, so you always get one. Rain and heads can both happen or not happen.

opts: Picking a blank from 8 stars and 2 blanks
Picking a blank from a tumbler of only star slips
quiz.why: If there are no blank slips, a blank can never come out. A crow at the window and picking a blank from 8 stars and 2 blanks can both happen.

quiz.p: Jyoti and her sister want to choose who goes first. Which way is fair?
opts: Jyoti goes first if a die shows 1 to 5
Toss a coin: heads for Jyoti, tails for her sister
Jyoti always goes first because she is older
quiz.why: A coin gives each sister the same chance. The die rule gives Jyoti five faces and her sister one.

quiz.p: A tumbler has 8 star slips and 2 blank slips. How can you make it fair for a star player and a blank player?
opts: Make the numbers of star and blank slips the same
quiz.why: With the same number of each, a star and a blank have the same chance. More star slips would make it even less fair.

quiz.p: Lakshmi tosses heads five times in a row. What is the chance of heads on the next toss?
opts: Less than before, because tails is due
The same as before, half and half
More than before, because heads is on a run
quiz.why: Each toss starts fresh. The last five tosses do not change how the next one spins and lands. Thinking tails is due is a very common mistake.

quiz.p: Pooja tosses a coin 10,000 times. What will the heads count be close to?
quiz.why: About half the tosses are heads, and the more tosses there are, the closer to half it usually gets. John Kerrich did this and got 5,067 heads.

applications: Weather scientists at the India Meteorological Department say how likely rain is, because they cannot know for sure. The physicist Anna Mani designed many of the weather instruments the department used.
In cricket, the two captains toss a coin, and the winner chooses to bat or bowl first. A coin gives both teams the same chance.
Board games such as Ludo and snakes and ladders use a die, so nobody can choose how far to move.
Doctors test a new medicine on many people, not just one, because one person's result can be a fluke, but many together show what usually happens.
Lucky draws at school fairs pick a name without looking, so every ticket has the same chance.

open_questions.q: If we knew exactly how a coin was tossed, could we always say how it would land?
open_questions.why_open: A machine built to toss a coin the same way every time can make it land the same way every time. But nobody can measure a hand toss that exactly. Scientists still argue about how much of chance is only what we cannot measure.

open_questions.q: Why do so many people feel that tails is due after many heads?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists who study minds have found that people expect short runs to look evenly mixed. They are still finding out why minds expect this.

open_questions.q: Is anything in nature truly a matter of chance?
open_questions.why_open: The tiniest particles seem to behave by chance. Some physicists think this chance is real. Others think there are hidden rules we have not found. Nobody has settled it.

maths.problem: In the coin test, Ananya made a tally of her heads. It has two bundles of five lines and one more single line. How many heads did she get?
maths.explain: Each bundle is 5. Two bundles make 10, and one more line makes 11.
maths.context: This question is about the coin test. You guessed ten tosses of a coin, then each person tossed a coin 20 times and counted the heads.
maths.why_maths: A tally keeps count while you toss, and bundles of five make it quick to add up at the end.

maths.problem: Ananya got 11 heads in 20 tosses. Her Amma got 9 heads in 20 tosses. How many heads did they get altogether, out of 40 tosses? Is that close to half?
maths.answer: 20 heads out of 40. That is exactly half.
maths.explain: 11 and 9 make 20. Half of 40 is 20. One count was a little over half and one a little under, and together they balanced out.
maths.context: This question is about the coin test. You guessed ten tosses of a coin, then each person tossed a coin 20 times and counted the heads.
maths.why_maths: Adding tosses together shows that the more tosses you count, the closer to half the total usually comes.

maths.problem: A die has six faces. How many faces are not a six? So which is more likely on one roll: a six, or not a six?
maths.answer: 5 faces are not a six, so not a six is more likely.
maths.explain: 6 faces take away the 1 face with a six leaves 5. Five faces against one face makes 'not a six' much more likely.
maths.context: This question is about the six test. You rolled a die 30 times and made a tally of sixes and not-sixes.
maths.why_maths: Counting the faces lets you work out which is likely before you even roll.

maths.problem: Nandini has 10 slips. 7 have a star. How many are blank? If she picks one without looking, is a star likely or unlikely? What should she change to make a star and a blank just as likely?
maths.answer: 3 are blank. A star is likely. She should make 5 star slips and 5 blank slips.
maths.explain: 10 take away 7 is 3. There are more star slips than blank ones, so a star is likely. With 5 of each, the chances are the same.
maths.context: This question is about the slips game. You put 8 slips with a star and 2 blank slips in a tumbler, and picked one without looking, ten times.
maths.why_maths: Counting what is in the tumbler tells you what is likely to come out, and how to make a game fair.

roots.context: We have tossed coins, rolled a die and picked slips without looking. Now we ask what chance tells us about the world, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: You could not say how any one toss would land. Yet each person's 20 tosses gave close to 10 heads. Each toss was unknown, but the total came out nearly the same each time. So we can know a lot about many tosses without knowing any single one.
deep_truth.habit: We think that if we cannot know what will happen, we know nothing about it. The coin test shows that not knowing each toss still leaves a lot we can know about the total.
deep_truth.evidence: In the coin test, guesses about single tosses were right only about half the time. Yet each person's 20 tosses gave a heads count close to 10.

three.who_am_i: You cannot know what will happen tomorrow. But you can know what is likely, and get ready for it, like taking an umbrella in the monsoon.
three.what_is_life: No one can say which seed from a plant will land where they can grow. But a plant gives many seeds, so some are likely to find a good place.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of single happenings nobody can know, like each raindrop and each toss. Together they make patterns we can count on.

roots.thread: Each toss on its own is a surprise. Put many together, and a steady pattern appears: close to half heads. That pattern is not in any one toss. It shows up only when many tosses are counted together. Everything is conscious, including the coin and the die, each in their own way. Many scientists disagree, and say awareness belongs only to living beings with brains.

teachings.teaching: Krishna tells Arjuna that his part is the action itself, and that the result is not his to hold on to.
teachings.link: In the coin test, you could choose how to shake the tumbler, but not how the coin landed. Your part was the toss and the honest count.

teachings.source: Jain thought, syadvada (the teaching of 'maybe', part of anekantavada)
teachings.teaching: Jain thinkers taught people to begin a claim with 'syat', which means 'in some way' or 'maybe'. This keeps us from saying more than we really know.
teachings.link: Saying 'heads is likely' or 'a six is unlikely' is the same kind of careful speaking. It says what we know, and no more.

science.text: The more times something is tried, the closer the count usually comes to its chance. Jacob Bernoulli first proved this, in a book published in 1713. It is called the law of large numbers.
A coin tossed by hand lands on the side that started on top about 51 times in 100. A team found this in 2023 by tossing coins over 350,000 times.

other_view.who: Albert Einstein, in a letter to the physicist Max Born in 1926
other_view.view: Einstein wrote that he was sure God does not throw dice. He meant that underneath, nature has no real chance at all, only causes we have not found.

practice.title: Holding not-knowing

practice.kid: Toss the coin. Cover it before you look. Close your eyes. Breathe slowly. Nobody knows yet. How does that feel? Now look.

playtest: Thought through as a parent and child in a flat. The coin test needs one coin, a steel tumbler and a bed or towel. Shaking the coin in a covered tumbler and tipping it onto a bed works for a child of 7, who cannot yet flip a coin with a thumb, and the bed stops it rolling under furniture. Twenty tosses with a tally take about 3 to 4 minutes per person. Guesses come out right about half the time, usually 3 to 7 of 10. Twenty tosses give 7 to 13 heads nearly 9 times in 10, so the 'close to 10' result is clear. The six test gives about 5 sixes in 30 rolls, usually 2 to 8, against 22 to 28 not-sixes, so the difference is easy to see. A six-sided pencil with numbers written on its sides works if there is no die.
